zone: Rainy Pass, Maple Pass and Easy Pass
_areas_note: TWO trailheads on SR 20, eleven road miles apart, and they do not connect on foot. (1) The Rainy Pass west lot at the Heather-Maple Pass loop serves Black Peak and Corteo Peak by way of Heather Pass, Lewis Lake and Wing Lake; both summits are climbed off the same string of camps, and Corteo is normally taken from the Lewis Lake moraine over a notch on the ridge east of it rather than by any line of its own. (2) The Easy Pass trailhead between mileposts 151 and 152 serves the whole Ragged Ridge group — Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva. All four were verified as Easy Pass peaks: Katsuk sits about 0.4 mile west of Mesahchie on the same crest, Kimtah is further west again and is almost never climbed on its own, and Arriva stands about a mile and a half southwest of the pass. No peak was excluded. THE LAND BOUNDARY IS THE POINT OF THIS FILE and it runs straight through it: the top of Easy Pass IS the line between Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest and North Cascades National Park, so every Ragged Ridge camp is inside the park and needs a park backcountry permit, while Black Peak's summit sits on that same boundary but Lewis and Wing Lakes lie on the FOREST side and need no permit at all. Nothing here duplicates the Cutthroat Creek file, which covers a different trailhead and the developed campgrounds down-valley from it. The Ragged Ridge traverse container was added after a later pass: it is not a summit but its one route traverses Ragged Ridge, which this file Easy Pass camps serve.

sites.name: Wing Lake
sites.capacity: A handful of established pads in the boulders and heather around the outlet, most taking one or two tents. It is the best ground on this side of the peak and it fills on clear summer weekends and hard in larch season, so have Lewis Lake in mind as the fallback.
sites.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the season. Snow patches under Black Peak feed it well into the autumn. Filter or treat.
sites.permit: None. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, not the national park, so there is no backcountry permit, no quota and nothing to reserve. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass covers parking at Rainy Pass. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine from mid summer onward and at this elevation there is almost nothing to burn anyway, so plan on a stove and check the current order rather than assuming a fire is legal.
sites.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Black Peak and the natural first night for Corteo as well. From the Rainy Pass west lot the loop trail is followed for a little over a mile, then a right fork leads to Heather Pass; from there a boot path crosses a boulder field and drops to Lewis Lake, and a further climb of about twelve hundred feet up the northwest slope reaches Wing Lake in the cirque under Black Peak. Reckon on four to six hours with a pack, and four to seven more from camp to summit and back. Camping here rather than at Lewis costs an hour on the way in and buys a much shorter summit day, which matters because everything above is talus and heather with route-finding rather than trail. The boundary detail is worth knowing: Black Peak's summit stands on the line between the forest and the national park, but this camp is on the forest side, so a party sleeping here needs no permit even though it is climbing a peak the park shares.

sites.name: Lewis Lake
sites.capacity: A few sites around the shore, fewer and rougher than Wing Lake's. Adequate for a party or two, and the obvious answer when Wing is full or when weather turns on the way up.
sites.water: The lake and its inlet run all season. Reliable.
sites.permit: None — national forest, no permit, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Rainy Pass.
sites.notes: Lewis sits in the bowl below Wing, reached by dropping off Heather Pass and picking a way through talus on goat paths around the left-hand shore. Most parties treat it as a waypoint rather than a destination, but it is a genuine camp and a sensible one for a late start, a heavy pack or a party that wants a shorter first day. It is also where the Corteo approach commits: from here the line follows the top of the moraine onto the Lewis Glacier and climbs southeast, bearing left at the top, to a notch on the ridge near seven thousand five hundred feet, then works west along the ridge and downclimbs several hundred feet of dirt or snow into the cirque under Corteo's west face, gaining the southwest ridge at a large notch by an easy gully. Nothing above Lewis is trail. Snow lingers on the traverse out of Heather Pass into early summer and an axe is worth carrying until it has gone.

sites.name: Rainy Pass trailhead lots, and the quarter-mile camping closures
sites.capacity: Two large paved lots either side of the highway, with the Maple Pass loop starting from the west side. They fill early on summer and autumn weekends. This is staging and roadside parking, not a campground.
sites.water: None at the pass. Fill in the valley or plan on filtering from the lakes once you are in.
sites.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. The rule that catches people out is a camping closure rather than a permit: no overnight camping within a quarter mile of Lake Ann, Rainy Lake, Heather Pass or Maple Pass, and none anywhere along the Heather-Maple Pass loop trail itself. Walk through to Lewis or Wing and you are legal with no paperwork; stop short of them and you are not.
sites.notes: This is the door to Black Peak and Corteo and the reason both are approachable in a weekend. It is also where the Pacific Crest Trail heads north, so the lots serve two entirely different sets of objectives and are busier than their size suggests. The closures above exist because the loop is one of the most walked trails in the state and its meadows were being trampled; they are enforced rather than advisory. Parties commonly sleep in the car here before an early start, and there is a toilet but no water. Everything depends on SR 20 being open — the highway shuts for the winter, usually in late November or early December, and reopens after avalanche control and snow clearing, most often between mid April and early May but occasionally very much later when a hard winter leaves washouts and rockslide damage behind it. Confirm the road is actually open before driving out from either side, and expect construction closures on this stretch in some seasons.

sites.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
sites.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.
sites.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
sites.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
sites.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs may come only as far as the pass, because the top of the pass is the national park boundary.

sites.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
sites.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.
sites.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
sites.permit: NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
sites.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.

sites.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
sites.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.
sites.water: SEASONAL AND OFTEN GONE. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
sites.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
sites.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.

sites.name: Fisher Camp, Fisher Creek basin
sites.capacity: Three designated sites — two taking a single tent each and one that will hold about four. A privy is provided. Being a named camp rather than a zone, it is reserved specifically and can simply be full.
sites.water: Fisher Creek, right at the camp, and it runs all season. This is the most reliable water anywhere on the Ragged Ridge side.
sites.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required and reserved for this specific named site, not for a zone. Book in advance through the national online system and collect the permit from park staff shortly before the trip. Food must be stored properly; a canister is the simplest answer. No campfires, and no dogs anywhere beyond Easy Pass.
sites.notes: Fisher Camp sits in the forested basin west of and well below Easy Pass, reached by carrying on over the pass and descending into Fisher Creek. It is the comfortable option and it is also the alternative approach to Kimtah that some parties prefer: rather than the long sidehill traverse along the south flank of Ragged Ridge, they drop into the basin, losing something like eighteen hundred feet, and then climb a more direct line straight back up to the crest. Whether that trade is worth it depends on snow on the traverse and on how much the party dislikes scree. Further down the valley the trail passes additional designated camps toward the Thunder Creek junction, which is how a Ragged Ridge trip can be finished as a through-hike rather than an out-and-back. The descent to this camp is real elevation that has to be regained on the way out, and it is the reason a summit-focused party stays high instead.
